utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we ask the witness to re-enter the courtroom, I still owe a decision on the admission of document D110 tendered by the Defence. That is a letter of the 2nd of February, 1993, by Marcetic, addressed to Colonel Cutler. The Chamber admits D110 into evidence. The witness, Mr. Cutler, has identified the letter as the one he received from Mr. Marcetic. The Chamber takes note that the witness testified that he had not seen any heavy weaponry on Mount Igman. His testimony does not contain a confirmation of the presence of the weaponry mentioned on the locations indicated in the letter, but the testimony did include that he had seen locations on Mount Igman that had the appearance of being prepared to have heavy weaponry positioned there. [Real-time transcript read in error "appeared to have heavy weaponry positions there."] This is the decision in this respect. Mr. Ierace, are you ready to resume the examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is two matters that I wish to raise but before I raise those, I notice that the transcript of your comments at line 18 in the English contains the words, "locations on Mount Igman that appeared to have heavy weaponry positions there."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I said is: "The appearance of being prepared."

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, there are two issues I seek to raise before we commence the evidence today. The first harks back to comments that I made yesterday to the effect that we may have a problem with the witnesses for the Prosecution later this week. We had anticipated that Christian Bergeron would give evidence after Paul Southwell and before Francis Thomas. He is travelling from Canada, and it now seems extremely unlikely that he will be here, in effect, in two days' time. Enquiries have been made as to whether we could bring forward Richard Mole or interpose a witness further down the list. Both of those attempts have been unsuccessful. I therefore anticipate at this stage that the evidence for this week will conclude with Francis Thomas, which may well be before the close of the session on Friday. I will continue to make attempts to bring someone in at the last minute, at least to give their evidence in chief, so as not to disadvantage the Defence. Mr. President, the second matter is I raised with you last week, the issue of some submissions in relation to Witness AD - I will be mindful that we are not in closed session - I asked if the Trial Chamber preferred written -- a written response from the Prosecution or oral submissions. If you wish to have written submissions, they could be now filed very shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I, since, of course, the submission has -- submissions by the Prosecution in response to what has been filed until now?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would have prepared it, of course, it could be filed. The Chamber has no specific preference, apart from one preference that we use the time in court as efficiently as possible. So, if you have prepared anything in response -- but there is one thing I first want to consider. We had a motion, we had a decision, we had a further submission from the Defence. Let me, during the first break, give you -- after the first break, let me give you the feeling of the Chamber on whether we would need an additional round of views or not. So if you could wait for one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President. And it occurs to me that given it is unlikely that we can fill the anticipated gap later this week, perhaps we could make use of that time by applying it to any outstanding issues which require discussion in court. I have in mind, for instance, a certain view. I won't say any more in public session. There are some other issues as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we could fill in the gap in the end of the week by these issues, I can assure you that the Chamber will be prepared for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And perhaps in that regard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So perhaps the parties will be prepared for it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Thank you for letting me take the floor. There are two comments I would like to make. With your permission, you will see me wearing sunglasses occasionally. It is not for stylistic reasons. It's just a problem that I have, and I don't want to be too affected by the screens. And the second problem is this, Mr. President, with regard to the witness that we are cross-examining. We received supplementary documents not only which date from yesterday, but which date from the day before yesterday, before the examination of the witness commenced. This isn't the first time that we have been racing against the clock in this courtroom, and the Defence would like to emphasise that it can no longer ensure such a Defence in a reasonable manner if, on each occasion, a few hours and sometimes a few minutes before a hearing, if not after the beginning of the hearing, we are provided with such information. And this is quite contrary to the Rule 65 ter. If I am saying this in a troubled voice, it is because I am very tired, Mr. President, in all senses of that term, because we have also received for the witness O'Keefe, who should be appearing very soon, we have received a binder in which there are I don't know how many documents and it is impossible for us to seriously present these documents to Mr. Galic because this binder was given to us yesterday, I think, in the course of the day, in the ad hoc file. So it is quite impossible to ensure a Defence of such importance if on each occasion we are provided with documents or information which are not just recent but which are absolutely recent. And I think we have to know what is wanted. The procedure has to be respected and then everyone will be content or we will be racing against time and, as I say, this is a violation of the Defence's rights, and I have mentioned this already. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. You made some observations in general terms on the documents you received. Since you indicated that these are a large number of documents, I think it was just about for you to do so. As you may have also noticed during the past few months, very often, if it comes to specific documents, the Chamber waits and see what is the document about, what is new about it, and to be in a better position to assess what prejudice it would have on the Defence preparation of the case. So what I would like to do now is to give Mr. Ierace an opportunity to respond to the general observations, so not to any specific documents because we will deal with that if they turn up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Firstly, in relation to the supplemental information which was provided to the Defence, I think yesterday, together with a draft translation, that document contains two pieces of information. The first is a change of date which appears in the statement. The second is some information in relation to an unscheduled shelling incident which the witness witnessed, he personally observed. I note that the first time that the Defence has complained about the receipt of supplemental information sheets was in respect of the witness Lieutenant-Colonel Cutler. It is a procedure which we have followed throughout the trial, and again I state that the only reason that these are received by the Defence at the last moment in some cases is because we receive information at the last minute. And it is, to my mind, the fairest possible way to make that information available to the Defence and I think it is important that we do make it available to the Defence, whether it is inculpatory or exculpatory. Mr. President, in relation to the second concern of my friend, that is the documents he has received in respect of the witness O'Keefe, most of those documents -- first of all, all of those documents have previously been disclosed. Secondly, most of the documents, if not all - certainly most - will not ultimately be tendered but rather will be shown to the witness and his attention will be drawn to a particular sentence or a few words, in the same way as the Prosecution has done with the last half dozen witnesses or so. If it would assist my friend, if he would care to return the folder, then perhaps tomorrow morning, before court, I could mark for him the particular sentences or groups of words that we propose to take the witness to so as to enable him to more quickly become familiar with that material. That assumes that we don't get to Mr. O'Keefe today, and I must say there is a strong likelihood that we will. Mr. President, I guess the other way of doing it is this: It will become apparent to my friend in examination-in-chief, of course, which are the relevant words or sentences, and if he needs time to obtain instructions in relation to those passages, perhaps an adjournment, given we have time at the end of the week anyway, an adjournment until tomorrow, then the Prosecution would certainly consider its position in relation to that. It may well agree to it, depending on what my learned friend seeks. Yes, that is the position of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you for allowing me to take the floor very briefly, once again. However interesting it may be, I think that Mr. Ierace's submission fails to take into consideration one of the Defence's fundamental rights, and that is to find out which are the documents for the Defence. And I don't think that in this brief lapse of time we can find documents for the Defence since General Galic doesn't have access to them. I know that the accusation likes to prepare phrases and submit them but, unfortunately, it is not possible for them to do that with the Defence. That is not the goal of this procedure here. The goal of this procedure is to detect, discover the truth, and we won't be able to do so unless we have time to follow the procedure. With regard to the disclosure, the anterior disclosure of documents, I would like to say that if it had been done in an electronic way, I know how difficult it would be -- I know how difficult it is to retrace these documents, and I don't want to refer to preceding cases. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you wish it, I can make some enquiries as to whether these documents have been disclosed in hard copy form as well as electronic form previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are these documents listed under the exhibit numbers or are they not? So apart from whether you intend to tender them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked the question to Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, another member of the Prosecution team prepared this. I anticipate the answer is yes, but I will check. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I would just like to say that we wrote a letter a few days ago and addressed it to Mr. Ierace, and a copy was submitted to the register. And we said we had verified this matter. We haven't seen a large number of documents listed in the Prosecution's ad hoc document. There are no contestations about this fact. I was then provided with a new binder with this document by the Prosecution, and I am grateful for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it seems the documents that my friend has were first listed to the Defence on the 21st of May, being some seven days ago. I must say, I am not sure what my learned colleague meant by the last passage, according to the English translation. But perhaps it is better, since he seems to hint at some earlier correspondence in relation to these very documents, perhaps it is better that I check with the relevant member of my team before we take this matter further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if you do that during the first break, Mr. Ierace. So we will hear from the Prosecution after the break when Mr. Ierace has further information from a colleague of his team who prepared the documents and who might have seen the correspondence. Then I think it is time - it is already late - for asking Mr. Niaz to enter the courtroom. Mr. Usher, would you please escort Mr. Niaz into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Niaz, good afternoon. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise that you had to wait, but we had to deal with a few procedural issues. That is what happens now and then in a courtroom. But you -- the Prosecution will now resume your examination. Mr. Ierace, please proceed. May I remind you, Mr. Niaz, perhaps it is not necessary, that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave yesterday at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Niaz, yesterday you told us the names of the areas, that is some of the areas, which came under your observation as a Papa side UNMO. Did any of those areas contain what might be described as predominantly residential areas?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. Most of the areas in my area of responsibility was predominantly residential area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: During the time that you were an UNMO in Sarajevo, that is, from the 2nd of October, 1993 until March 1994, could you tell us something of the consistency or inconsistency of sniping activity in those areas?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as for the sniping activities concerned, were most of the time consistent and we could see the -- most of the time, we could hear these snipings coming in from the Grbavica side and a lot of injuries --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please repeat those last few words of your answer?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, a lot of injuries and a lot of casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you say that you heard sniping coming from the Grbavica side, on which side of the confrontation lines was that part of Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the south-western part -- south-eastern part.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Which forces controlled that area at the relevant times?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That area was controlled by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What about the shelling over the period of time that you were in Sarajevo, were there days or weeks when there was more shelling than at other times?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, there are no -- we could not specify that these would be certain days in a week when there was more shelling or there were certain days in a week when there were little shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If I could interrupt you there. What I mean is, were there some periods where there were more shelling or less shelling than at other times?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I remember one day very directly, and that happens to be 16th of October, 1993. And during my tenure, that was probably the heaviest shelling which we counted inside the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How many shell landings did you count within the confrontation lines on that day?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not the confrontation line, but the shells, most of the shells landed inside the city. And I think the time I started counting, and if I finished counting, was about 1500, 2000 rounds, and thereafter we lost count of the rounds. And in fact, I have given a detailed account of this --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. I will stop you there. Are you aware as to whether there were any civilian casualties that day from that shelling?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least -- I was that day or midday, I was stuck up in the Kosevo hospital emergency ward because we had no other place to go out. It was not safe for us to be in any part of the city. So first two casualties which I saw there coming was an old woman. I have given a photograph of that also.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Can I stop you there? First of all, could you please slow down with your answers so that the transcriber can keep up with you? Secondly, can you focus on simply whether you are aware as to how many civilian casualties there were that day as a result of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 11, roughly 11, that, and about 20 or 23 injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: From the Kosevo hospital, were you able to see any of the explosions in the city?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, initially, we were in the emergency ward where we could only hear it. But I used to try to get out, to see where it was safe for us to get out and move back to our OP. So, during that time, I did see quite a number of rounds land inside the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: At what time, if you remember it, did this shelling start on that day?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shelling started precisely at about 0400 hours in the morning. At that time, we were in our OP.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you remember whether it seemed to finish at a particular time?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It finished up at about between 1500 hours to probably 1600 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, speaking generally about the shelling during the period you were in Sarajevo, did you notice whether there was any pattern or correlation between periods of shelling of the city and other events?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: From time to time, were you able to see a connection, any connection, between the shelling of the city and other events that were happening perhaps elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At times, when we could hear heavy exchange of small arm fire on the southern part of confrontation line, and immediately after that we saw a heavy concentration of the shelling inside the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: During the period you were in Sarajevo, were there any offensives carried out by the Bosnian government troops anywhere along the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not particularly aware of such incident but -- because I did not see them myself. But from the exchange of the artillery, from the exchange of the small arm fires, we did presume that there were certain offensives which were carried out by the -- both the sides, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You've told us that the intensity of the shelling was greater on some days than others. Were you able to work out a reason for any of the periods of intensive shelling of residential area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. It is very difficult, as we know, to define the town, what is a residential zone in it and what isn't. We know that very well. So I would like Prosecution to rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber finds no need to instruct Mr. Ierace to rephrase the question, but, of course, if the issue is of importance, it could be raised during cross-examination. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will repeat the question, Colonel. You told us that the intensity of the shelling was greater on some days than others. Were you able to work out a reason for any of the periods of intensive shelling of residential areas?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The possibilities which I could -- my UNMOs could work out was that whenever the Bosnian would go in for some offensive, to release the pressure from that particular area from that particular attack, they would ensure that there was a lot of shelling and sniping inside the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you personally witness any incidents where an individual or individuals who you regarded as indisputably civilians were shelled?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is there one particular incident that comes to mind?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One incident -- I, at this point of time, don't remember the dates or the days. We were going on a patrol and maybe about 250 yards on where we were proceeding--

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If I could just interrupt you there. Did you say you were going on a patrol?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were you in a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most of the patrol, apart from the confrontation or the front line, was carried out in the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we went in that vehicle and about 250 yards, that is my estimate at this time, a mortar bomb exploded --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sorry, was that a "mortar bomb"?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes a mortar bomb coming up, exploded, and we could see a woman and a child, she was a girl, going together and suddenly blown up. Now, at this particular moment, we took the vehicle at the site to see that first. We waited for about 6 to 10 minutes, to see that there was no further shelling. We proceeded up to the site. We collected the pieces of the body in two garbage bags and the civilians helped us out, and then we took them to the Kosevo morgue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, you have told us that you don't remember the particular date. Do you remember the month?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was definitely before the market incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: By that, which market do you mean?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Markale.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Markale?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell us the area where the incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you go -- I don't know whether I will be able to exactly point it out with a map. But if you go eastwards from the city centre, there is climb going up. The road starts ascending around both sides. It is a purely residential area. Both sides of the street are flats and houses. That was that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of the area?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly, I don't know -- I could find it on a map, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask the witness be shown a copy of the standard Prosecution map which I think has previously been referred to as P3644. I may or may not ask the witness to mark it, depending on his answers. It may not be necessary for him to mark it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace. Could you assist, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think, for the moment, it would have the exhibit number P3644AN, "N" for Nelly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please look at the map, Colonel, and tell us if you are able to identify on the map the place where the incident occurred. When you find the relevant area, if you do, with the assistance of the usher, could you place that part of the map on the machine in front of you?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The streets on the maps are not clear, but somewhere here. The streets are not clear. The moment you hit the city centre, there is a square and that road goes to the left --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If I could stop you there, please. You will notice that one of the four edges of the map has the name "Sarajevo." Do you see that, on the edge of the map?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Can you place the map so that edge is furthest away from you so that we can make more sense of the image on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you turn it 90 degrees to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It may be more convenient if the usher folds the map so only the relevant portion is on the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, if you could answer this question: Have you located on the map the position where you saw the woman and girl blown up?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was probably -- the streets are not clear. I think this is probably -- maybe this is probably. I may not be accurate, but this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please take a blue pen and place a cross --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this the only part you would like the witness to mark, because then perhaps we could do it in a more efficient way because we have, what I saw - if I am wrong, please correct me - I saw the witness pointing to an area on the map which is on the eastern side of the centre of the city just approximately one centimetre left from where the word "Kovaci" appears.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're right, sir. I would agree that if we could mark in an efficient way, in a map where the streets are a little more clearer. I may not be able to find the exact location, but that would be the general area, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be the area. If the witness would not come any closer, Mr. Ierace, do you think --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That will do, Mr. President, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Niaz, we might have heaps of maps finally marked by everyone. I think it's quite clear -- since this is the only marking expected from you, I think it's now clearly indicated where you located the area where it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Colonel, approximately how far from the confrontation line did the incident take place?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the eastern side of Sarajevo. The confrontation line from this place was quite far off. Maybe -- I may be wrong, but 5 kilometres, maybe more.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You have told us that you had done some training in crater analysis. Did you carry out an analysis of this particular crater?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were you able to determine the direction from which the mortar -- along which the mortar had travelled?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was that direction?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was generally from the direction of Sedrenik. We used to call it "steep" or "sharp stones," that area, in the UNMO terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were you able to determine the size of the mortar shell based on your observations?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, at that time we were -- the incident was such that it was probably even different than -- it was a shock for all of us but -- I may be wrong, but it was probably a 120-millimetre mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you say that it was a shock for all of you, what you had witnessed?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, you described one of the two females as being a girl. Approximately how old was she?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not more than 9. Between 8 and 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what sort of clothing they were wearing at the time, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am trying to follow the English transcript. I don't see that it is reflects -- I am not sure whether it reflects what the witness said, whether he said "direct shock" or "direct shot" because it is not in the transcript. I did not hear clearly what he said, and I think it is important to clarify this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is why I asked the question which appears at line 2 on page 18, to clarify that it was indeed "shock."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I heard the witness confirm that he talked about a shock. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was the nature of the area? How would you describe it in terms of -- and socially? In other words, was it an industrial area, commercial area or what?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This area was then purely a residential area, with a few or a couple odd shops.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Approximately how far was your vehicle from the two females at the time that they were killed?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 250, to maximum 300.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Metres or yards or what?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yards.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, did you see anyone near them, that is, anyone at all?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were going on the right side of the road and maybe one or couple civilians because -- could be on the other side or the same side. I don't remember because the moment this thing happened, about 5 or 6 of them gathered. I presumed that they were also in the near vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did any of them have anything about their appearance that could be interpreted as denoting them as combatants?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can remember neither were they policeman or neither were they in the army uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, what about your vehicle? Did it have any markings on it?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All our vehicles were white in colour with very clear UN in blue, and most of the time we had our flags on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you see in the area of the two females anything that could be regarded or even mistaken as military equipment or weaponry?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will now take you to a different topic, namely, the incident at Markale market in February of 1994. Had you seen the market on that day but before the explosion?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, that was in my daily patrol route.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you notice the number of people at the market on that day before the explosion?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time was between 9.00 and 10.00 and it was crowded.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you say "it was crowded," can you give us some idea of how crowded it was?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would be difficult for me to give you the exact figures, but if I use the word it was "jam packed."

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think that communicates some sense of how crowded. What time -- I think you said it was between 9.00 and 10.00 a.m. that you noticed it to be jam packed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: At some stage later did you hear an explosion?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Where were you, in relation to the market, at the time that you heard that explosion?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after carrying out a morning patrol inside the city and submitting our daily report to the Papa headquarters, we went back to our OP. Our OP is -- was located, that is Papa 2, in area known as Hum, H-u-m. It is just below the famous TV tower overlooking the city. So we were having lunch, we just started lunch. Once we heard an explosion inside the city, as a normal operation procedure, one of my UNMO went out, give the general direction of the incoming mortar or incoming explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If I could ask you to clarify that you said that, pursuant to normal operation procedure, one of your UNMOs gave the general direction of the incoming mortar or incoming explosion. Do you mean by that that one of your UNMOs established the direction from which the sound of the explosion came or do you mean something else?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this case, we were sitting at a predominant height, at an OP which used to be overlooking the city. We used to presume or estimate the general direction of the fire and the place -- the general place, not an exact place, where the explosion had landed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On this -- in this case, did your UNMO determine the direction of the resulting explosion or something else?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he pointed out the general direction of -- then, from the general direction of Sedrenik, but he was not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: At this stage, you are -- you were at Papa 2; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Did you go to the marketplace?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, why did you go to the marketplace? How did you know to go there?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Papa headquarters was located inside the city, quite near to the marketplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So did you receive a phone call or a radio message or something of that order?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received a phone call and an immediate message to leave everything and report to the place of explosion which we had reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now I think you told us that you heard what you believe to be the sound of the explosion at the marketplace; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. How long was it -- withdraw that. At approximately what time did you hear that explosion?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may be wrong, it is a long time --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If you don't remember --

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe 12.00, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You say "maybe 12.00." Having regard to your earlier words, do you mean that you are not sure if that was the time?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be correct, I may not be correct in giving you the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. If you are not sure of any answer that you give, please tell us, do you understand?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, approximately how long after you heard that explosion did you arrive at the market?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maximum 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you arrived at the market, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived at the market, the police, the local police was already there. They have -- they had cordoned off the area. There were one or two French UNPROFOR APCs standing there and the place was littered with bodies, blood. The tempers of the locals were very high, especially once I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were you wearing your uniform?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did that uniform indicate that you were part of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had a helmet, blue helmet, with "UN" written on the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were angry words said to you?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the moment I entered, I went inside the cordoned area -- to a police officer, took out a leg of a victim and shouted: "Boutros-Ghali, happy New Year."

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was that a severed leg?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and if I am not wrong, this incident was shown for quite some time on the Sky TV probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Without going into detail, is it fair to say that there were a number of comments made to you by people present, expressing anger at the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, did you notice -- you told us that you saw bodies. Did you see anyone there who was apparently wounded, but alive?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was myself ordered by the Senior Military Observer, Major Thomas Roy, to bring on whatever casualty I can inside the PTT building French hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, firstly, did you go to the market with some other people?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had two vehicles. I had Captain Simon Guest.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is "Guest" spelled G-u-e-s-t?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. From the Royal Marines. Major -- Captain Mubarek -- sorry, Captain Mubarek from Jordan.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is "Mubarek" spelled M-o-u-b --

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: M-u-b. M-u-b-a-r-e-k. Almost right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Major Farouk from Bangladesh, and the interpreter Jasmina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The interpreter, was that Jasmina?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was there anyone else that you recollect at this stage?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We left one -- and probably a Dutch UNMO. I am not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the Dutch UNMO that you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you provide any assistance upon your arrival to the victims?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because that was the priority then given to me by the SMO, that I must assist and regulate the location of casualties from the scene of incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And did you assist with the evacuation of any of the victims?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I myself took a woman. She was an elderly woman, maybe late 50s, and probably a young boy. There were two of them. One -- this old woman was taken by me in my own vehicle and the other was taken by the other UNMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, whereabouts did you take that woman?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We took her to the PTT building, the headquarters of United Nations at Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We have heard evidence that there was a medical facility at the PTT building at some stage. Was that where you took her on this day?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I told you earlier that I was told by my SMO, the Senior Military Observer, that he had made arrangements with the French to receive the casualties. So otherwise the civilians were not allowed inside the PTT building. So he had arranged so that I was not stopped on the way, even at the initial barricade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that part of your duties in relation to the shelling of civilians in Sarajevo was to check the casualties or at least the casualty numbers. Did you do that in relation to this shelling of Markale?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And when did you do that? Was it that day or later?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. And what time did you start that process on that day?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I am correct, it was after 1700 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: 1700 hours, after that. Where were the places you went to in order to count the wounded and dead?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only one morgue in the Kosevo hospital, the Kosevo hospital itself. And in the city they had -- what did they call it? State hospital. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And what about the PTT French medical facility?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only took the casualties there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you counted the numbers, did you include those who were taken to the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. So you have mentioned the Kosevo hospital and Kosevo morgue, the state hospital, the PTT medical facility. Were there any other medical facilities that you checked for casualties that day that you now recollect?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How many dead did you count that day which you understood to be fatalities from that market explosion?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exact figures, I may not be remembering, but between 60 to 70 were dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And wounded?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now you have told us -- withdraw that. When you described the area of the city that was under your observation, I think you said the city centre. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What part of the city would you regard Markale as being in at that stage?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the city centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Since you had been in Sarajevo, that is, from the 2nd of October, 1993, until the day of the market explosion, were you aware of any other -- of any mortars falling within, say, a radius of 200 metres of the marketplace?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Incidently, what is your recollection as to the date of the Markale market explosion? If you don't remember --

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Saturday, probably. It was Saturday or Sunday. For sure, it was a weekend, and 5th of February, 1994. I may be wrong, but this is what my recollection says.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, between the 2nd of October, 1993 and the 5th of February, 1994, approximately how many mortar rounds fell in a radius of 200 metres of the marketplace, approximately?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one which I saw and my team members saw along with me were between 10, 11, maybe 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now as a result of the crater analyses, were you -- are you able to tell us approximately how many of those involved a mortar of the size of 120 millimetre?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think most of them were 120-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, listen carefully to the question. I am asking you whether, in relation to those impacts that were analysed, whether you or your team with you were able to establish the direction that those mortars travelled, that is, the mortar impacts made since you had been in Sarajevo up until the 5th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. What was the direction?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general direction, and especially this part of the city, was from the Sedrenik side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you mean that if you drew a line on a map between the marketplace and Sedrenik, then that was the approximate direction of the mortar impacts, the craters? I am sorry, the direction along which the mortars which created those impacts had travelled; is that the case?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, finally, did you investigate an incident involving Kosevo hospital, where three or four people were killed in a shelling?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When did that incident occur?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact dates, but it was definitely before this market in maybe December or January.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As you understood it, how long before you arrived had the shelling or mortaring taken place?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When did I arrive? This question is not clear, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How long after the explosion did you arrive at Kosevo hospital to carry out your investigation?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kosevo hospital was -- you could see the Kosevo hospital through a very powerful binocular we had in our OP. So the moment I was reported upon this particular explosion, I think, another about 20 minutes to 30 minutes, we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you determine what type of missile had caused the explosion? In other words, was it an artillery shell, a mortar or something else?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this particular case, it had -- it had pierced -- it landed in, probably, in the first storey - I am not correct - of the hospital and we didn't see the impact, but we did see its -- the windows broken and from where the shell went inside. We did see certain splinters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If I could take you back to my question, and please tell me if your memory does not enable you to answer it: Were you able to determine what sort of missile caused it, and by "missile," I mean was it a mortar shell, an artillery shell, tank shell, what was it? If you don't remember, please say so.

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In that case, I won't ask you any more questions about that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you went past the -- drove past the marketplace between 9.00 and 10.00 a.m. on the 5th of February, were there any military vehicles near the market?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you -- correct, there were hardly any civilian or Bosnian vehicles inside the city on that particular day, obviously, no vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you notice any military equipment near the marketplace when you drove past between 9.00 and 10.00?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because it was part of our duty, the moment we observed a particular military vehicle went in an area, we would investigate and report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes the examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. Ms. Pilipovic or Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is the Defence ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Ready is a big word, but the Defence will cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. Can you hear me, sir?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, I am going to cross-examine you in French. My first question is as follows: Could you please tell this Trial Chamber what your religious origins are?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I object to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You object. Well, then I'll sit down. Good-bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't hear the last thing you said, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I will sit down. If this witness objects to this question, then there is no reason for me to ask it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no. Let's just first see, could you explain what the relevance is of your question, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Willingly, Mr. President. We know that in this conflict, and it's unfortunate, there were religious parties which were in conflict with each other. We know this very well. We know this witness stated that -- well, we know this witness stated that, in general, his team was composed of two persons, at least two persons. That was in what he stated yesterday, towards the end of the afternoon. We should at least know whether this witness had very firm religious convictions, that he was not just a layman, a secular person, and as a result, he might have a biased attitude. He might be biased towards one side than another and, as a consequence, he might not be objective. This is the only thing I wanted to talk about. And taking into account the statements he gave which contradicts some of the statements when he was asked whether certain fires -- certain shots could come from the Bosnian side, this witness replied to this question, categorically, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I certainly understand that it is the case for the Defence that there was a religious element to the conflict. I should make clear that that is not part of the Prosecution case. Indeed, we have led evidence that there were many members of other communities, including the Serbian community, who not only chose to stay in Sarajevo but contributed positively towards the defence of Sarajevo. My learned colleague went on in his explanation to suggest that if this witness has, to use my learned colleague's words, "very firm religious convictions," that that would somehow contribute towards bias on the witness's part. Mr. President, in my respectful submission, very firm religious convictions do not lead to a conclusion of bias. So, Mr. President, whilst I understand the Defence case, this aspect is not shared by the Prosecution. I now object to the question, having heard my friend's explanation because if bias is what he seeks to establish, then establishing the fact of the witness's religion and the degree of his religious conviction does not provide that basis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, to save time, I shall withdraw this question. I have seen how the witness reacted and that is sufficient for me. May I continue? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you are a Colonel, is that right?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you arrived in Sarajevo, you were just a major?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say, sir, that you were rapidly promoted to the rank of colonel?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not rapidly. I was a very senior major then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, no one is questioning the fact that -- sir, how much time did you require to become a colonel after having been a major?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 15 to 17 years, at the time, of getting promoted to the rank of lieutenant-colonel and 23 to 24 is the time of getting promoted to the rank of a full colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. I will ask you another question, sir: In your capacity as a superior officer, I think you are particularly well-versed in reading maps; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. I will show you a map a little later and will ask questions about it later on with regard to maps of Sarajevo, and I am going to ask you brief questions. If it is possible, can you answer "yes" or "no." Do you know where Zetra is?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time, I don't recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Do you know where Zitra is located?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you spell it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Z-i-t-s-a.

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: As a result, you don't know what could be located there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Do you know where Magro, M-a-g-r-o, is located and what might be at that location?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, do you know where the command and control post of the 102nd is located?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, do you know what Valter Peric is?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, would you by any chance know what Petar Dakic is?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Colonel, as a result, you are not in a position to know what might be located there, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, do you know where the 105th is located?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: 105th, what is 105th?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The 105th Brigade, not the 105th Avenue.

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Do you know where Pavle Goranin is located?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object to this staccato questioning with the gratuitous criticism reference to 105th Avenue. I take it my friend is referring to, I think what was called the 105th Motorised Brigade or some other fuller name. In my respectful submission, in the interest of relevance and probity, it should be put to the witness, the appropriate title should be put to the witness and there may be more revealing -- in other words, perhaps my friend should for a start put to the witness the full name of the relevant brigade. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since we are speaking to a military specialist who has spent more than a year in Sarajevo, we could base ourselves that on the principle that he knows what we are talking about when we are talking about the 105th or the 102nd, et cetera. I think that's quite clear. If I have to lose time by mentioning all the names, I'll do that willingly but we will be losing a lot of time for the accusation of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness asks for a clarification, which he did not on all the other questions you put to him, if he asks what 105th, in order to be sure what your question was about, I think you told him correctly that it was the 105th brigade. Whether this is the full name of the brigade, I don't think so, but I think it would have been proper to give him the information he asked for in order to answer your question. I think that the addition, "not the 105th Avenue" was not proper to do because we cannot blame the witness for asking clarification, if you just ask him where the 105th was located. Staccato or legato are the two, I would say the two ends of a line. Mr. Ierace asked, at least raised the issue that, staccato might not be the proper way of asking. I am not asking you to go to legato. But if you could find a way in between, it might sound well in all our ears. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With pleasure, Mr. President. I shall proceed moderata cantata as of now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, if you -- could you tell us where the Kulin Ban headquarters is, if you know where it is? K-u-l-i-n, and then the second word is B-a-n.

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness do you know where the Gras structures are located, G-r-a-s?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are Gras structures?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you repeat your comment please, Witness, because it hasn't appeared in full -- I see. Witness, do you know what Gras is, G-r-a-s?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In English, g-r-a double "s" or something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, we are speaking about Sarajevo and this is the name of something in Sarajevo. I fear that it is not in English. It is probably something in Serb.

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, can I consider that for each of the questions that I have asked you, in response to each these questions, you don't know what could be located in these places. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Witness, I would like to move on to another question that interests me which has to do with special units. Do you perhaps know anything about the existence of certain special units, for example, special units belonging to Drago Prazina?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, the same question for the Ljiljan group?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, the same question for the Kobra group.

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The same questions for the Fatih, Boris and Sultan Fatih groups. I will group them together.

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: As a result, you don't know where the control -- control and command posts of these special units were located, what in English is called the CC posts of these units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AFZAAL NIAZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Colonel. Mr. President, Your Honours, I think it might be a good time to have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Niaz, we will adjourn until a quarter past 4.00 and then the Defence will resume the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 4.18 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I made those enquiries over the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I am now in a position to given an explanation, if you want to hear it at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could do it briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yesterday, the Prosecution provided the Defence with draft translations of all of the contents of the documents which appeared on the exhibit list to be tendered through this witness on the 21st of May, 2002. As well as translations of those documents, the Prosecution provided translations of all of the documents referred to by the witness O'Keefe in his statement, even though we do not propose to tender those documents. Together with the translations, we provided Mr. Piletta-Zanin with English copies of the same documents, even though they had been disclosed to him at least since February and even though he had copies of those documents identified in the list provided to him seven days ago. We expressed to Mr. Piletta-Zanin that we were providing those English copies to assist him in determining the translations. So, Mr. President, I am completely at a loss to understand my friend's confusion. If you wish to see it, I have a copy of the letter which was faxed to the Defence on the 21st of May, 2002. That letter sets out in the usual fashion the dates on which the documents which are on the exhibit list were first disclosed, as well as the ERN numbers and the description. Mr. President, whilst I am on my feet, I anticipate there will be a supplemental information sheet provided in respect of the witness O'Keefe in the next short while which contains the contents of some information which he has provided to us for the first time in the last hour or so. That is about four lines long. If there is anything else you wish to hear from me in relation to the issue raised by my learned colleague this morning, I am able to do so. I am having steps to have brought to the Trial Chamber a copy of the letter which was included with the documents yesterday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first ask Mr. Piletta-Zanin if he could briefly indicate whether the facts just presented by Mr. Ierace are in any respect not correct. That is the first question I ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are not correct, Mr. President, to the extent that -- it is true that there was correspondence between the parties on the 21st of May, and immediately after that date, correspondence from the Defence to the Prosecution in which we asked for these documents. We were given binders which my colleague had, but there were documents which were missing, for technical reasons, and as soon as we were able to get ready for this witness -- because it wasn't possible to verify all the pages of all the documents, as soon as we started working on this witness, we immediately contacted the Office of the Prosecutor to say, stop, there is a problem; please disclose all the documents to us of which we do not have a copy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you: You made some complaints about that some documents were missing. Do I understand that some of the translations were still missing or some of the original documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. Mr. President, these are the originals in that we were basing ourselves on the letter that was disclosed to us by the Prosecution and in which the document numbers were mentioned. You have a divider and the number which is behind that. In the binder that we received, we only had one number, 974, and behind that number there were documents. The other numbers, they were either nonexistent, or in the case of one or two, there were dividers but there were no documents there. We immediately informed the Prosecution of this. Maybe it is just a technical problem of transmitting the documents, but as soon as we discovered this, we immediately informed the Prosecution of this problem. And have I been sufficiently clear, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was -- I am afraid that I still do not perfectly understand. You are provided with a letter and a lot of documents, and you said you couldn't identify all the documents in the binders you got. Were they then given to you when you complained about the incompleteness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, apparently, Mr. President, and I have to say, I would like to thank the Prosecution for this: As soon as the Prosecution discovered that there was a problem, they did its best in order to provide us with these documents as soon as possible. But we only received these documents very late and, to date, we have not been in a position to provide them to General Galic so that he can examine them, with the exception of document 974, which is the only document which we received at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When did you receive the translations of the other documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to ask my colleague who deals with these matters. Apparently, it was yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ierace, it is still a bit -- the information that comes to the Chamber is still a bit confusing. Is it true that the translation of at least a considerable number of documents - that does not necessarily mean the majority of the pages - but a considerable number of documents were only provided to the Defence yesterday or -- ?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes, some translations were provided to the Defence yesterday for the first time. They were draft translations of the entirety of the documents from which sentences would be taken, predictably in the evidence of Mr. O'Keefe, and also draft translations of documents attached to Mr. O'Keefe's statement, even though they are documents which the Prosecution does not intend to either tender or refer to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you are pointing at the limited use of these documents. When you say, "we are not going to tender," would the Prosecution -- could the Prosecution put questions it has in mind even without using those documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Theoretically, we could, of course, but we don't intend to. The reason it was done was because one might take the view that because a witness refers to a particular document in their statement, that that should be made available to the Defence. They were made available to the Defence in English. And so what we did yesterday, even though we don't intend to refer to them at all, was to provide the Defence with translations of them, nevertheless, as well as translations of the entirety of the documents on the exhibit list, even though the witness will only be taken to a line or two and even though most of them, if not all of them will not be tendered. My basic point, Mr. President, is that we have engaged in an exercise of assisting the Defence. We gave them a folder with the translations and additional English copies to help them, and in response, the Defence this morning has complained. Mr. President, if there is any concern on the part of the Trial Chamber, I think it is appropriate that Mr. Waespi be present because he was the lawyer dealing directly with Mr. Piletta-Zanin in relation to this matter. So that if any further issues are raised by my friend as has occurred in the last few minutes I'm able to respond straightaway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I know that we are looking at the clock, but to make things clearer because Mr. Ierace is here, I can respond. As regards to Mr. Francis Roy Thomas, a witness who will testify three hours, but perhaps less, there are about 10 exhibits which have been submitted by the Prosecution. For that witness who will be taking the stand in a while, no translations have been submitted. I am repeating this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, just one simple question: The documents Mr. Piletta-Zanin is referring to without translations, are they going to be tendered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, he is now referring to documents relating to a completely different witness. Some of those documents may well be tendered. They were identified yesterday. But when I say "may well be tendered," again, it is in the context of this recent procedure of simply showing them to the witness. Now, if they weren't on the exhibit list, if they were simply shown to the witness, there wouldn't be any requirement of us to provide a copy to the Defence or to have them translated, that is, if the witness was simply refreshing his memory from a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will slow down. So that is my response, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Let me just try to deal with both information sheets and documents that came up recently or have been provided additionally in B/C/S. It is the experience of this Chamber until now that discussing these kind of issues in general terms usually is not of great assistance to solve the problems. We discussed last week the issue of additional information sheets. So much depends on what is in there. If it is just a simple change from one date, from Tuesday until Wednesday, or the correction of a mistake, it is of no use to spend much time on general argument on additional information sheets. We have the experience that it is very often -- very often the same is true as far as documents are concerned. Sometimes it is easy to fully understand a document within two minutes and sometimes documents of the same length might take you three or four hours to fully understand it. For that reason, the Chamber, in respect of these new documents, first wants to reconfirm that the general rules are still standing, the list should be presented to the other party, but if for any unforeseen circumstances or for any other circumstances that might justify a deviation from the applicable rule, we will deal with that when this document or when this additional information comes up during the testimony of the witness. And if the Chamber is convinced that the Defence would need more time to prepare for cross-examination, such additional time will be granted as the Chamber, as far as our recollection goes, always granted additional time if really needed. I leave it to that at this very moment. Mr. Ierace, there is one other issue. You asked something at the beginning of this afternoon's session about any additional filing in respect of what I would call "AD." If you would file it, would you then do it as quickly as possible? And it is -- a motion has been, a response, so after this initial filing, unless the Chamber otherwise decides, there will be no further exchange of views until a final or a provisional decision will be given.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We will do that tomorrow morning, Mr. President. I have Mr. Waespi here now, if you wish there to be a response from the Prosecution in relation to what Mr. Piletta-Zanin has said transpired with missing documents and the like. Or if you think it is unproductive, then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I just said is that usually we get to a solution very quickly. If it comes to the specific document, then we can ask: When was this document, how much time would you need for this document, when was the translation given of this document, are you going to tender this specific document or not, in what way are you going to use it. And that is a far more productive way in the view of the Chamber to deal with these kind of matters. Mr. Piletta-Zanin

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, we shall conclude now because we don't find this to be extremely productive. I would like to underline one thing: As for supplementary information received yesterday regarding Colonel Niaz, I heard that the Prosecutor say that it was only a question of change of schedule. I note that in the two pieces of supplementary information for the very first time, and this was not earlier in the statement of the witness, the existence of shelling which was a subject of examination. There were dates, 17th and 18th of October, 1993, and it was impossible for the Defence to ask some questions to General Galic regarding those dates, about perhaps conflicts, and everything was done for us to make it impossible for us to ask these questions. I don't want to exhaust ourselves over --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you are saying is the additional information in respect of shelling on the 17th and 18th of October was never disclosed before, and then the next question is: Would you need more time to prepare for the cross-examination in that respect or would you like to interrupt the cross-examination then in order to have more time so that we could first continue with others? But before doing so, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Something very briefly, Mr. President. The dates of the 17th and 18th of October in relation to that unscheduled shelling incident were, in fact, not brought out by me in examination-in-chief. That was information which was in the supplemental information sheet which was provided with a translation sheet to the Defence yesterday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is not in my recollection. Were there any questions specifically to that date in the examination-in-chief? I haven't got it in my mind.
